title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback system can improve lesson planning in vocational teacher education. The authors focus on a practical problem in higher education: detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans is valuable for student teachers but difficult for university instructors to provide consistently and at scale. The study asks whether AI-based feedback can support or outperform human feedback on key didactic planning dimensions, and whether using such a system also influences students’ motivation, AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital competence, and technology self-efficacy.

The intervention centers on EDDA, an analytical AI platform that analyzes uploaded lesson plans and teaching materials using a BERT-based model trained on coded lesson plans and textbook tasks. EDDA does not generate open-ended responses like a large language model; instead, it classifies lesson plans into predefined didactic categories and returns expert-level text and visual feedback tied to established criteria. In the study, the experimental group used EDDA throughout a semester and could also consult the university instructor to discuss the AI feedback, while the control group received human feedback only. Both groups completed the same lesson-planning tasks and theoretical coursework.

The population consisted of 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working in small groups to design 90-minute vocational lessons. The intervention spanned a semester, with students iteratively incorporating six focal dimensions or principles into the same lesson plan: sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, and digitalization. Outcomes included coded analyses of lesson plans as well as repeated self-report surveys on AI literacy and related meta-dimensions.

The main conclusion is that analytical AI feedback can effectively supplement traditional instructor feedback and, on some lesson-planning dimensions, match or exceed human-only feedback. The experimental group showed advantages on selected planning aspects, including some sustainability-related dimensions, social competences for sustainable development, reflexivity, and several planning features highlighted in the abstract such as action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, or motivation. The authors therefore argue that analytical AI tools are promising for feedback in teacher education, but should be embedded in a broader, human-centered instructional framework rather than treated as a standalone solution.
